newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - U.S. fed funds seen rising 50 bps in '97.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - U.S. fed funds seen rising 50 bps in '97.

text.p: Inflation concerns will lead the Federal Reserve to raise short-term interest rates somewhat over the coming year, and the bond market probably will cheer the central bank's vigilance, according to a Reuters poll of 44 economists.
Although the odds of an interest-rate hike at the next Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting in March appear to be below 50 percent, most economists are calling for a tightening by June.
On average, the 44 experts forecast the federal funds target rate would move up from its current 5.25 percent rate to 5.50 percent by June and rise again, to 5.75 percent, by March 1998.

During the same survey period, the pundits project the bellwether 30-year Treasury bond's yield will increase from its current level of 6.82 percent, peaking at about 7.00 percent in September before falling back to about 6.80 percent by March 1998.
"All the numbers have been strong," said Charles Lieberman, chief economist at Chase Securities Inc.

"Everything from consumer spending, car spending, durable goods orders and initial claims -- the economy looks pretty healthy," he said, adding that last Friday's February payrolls data "added fuel to the fire."

Economists said Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan continues to fret over wage pressures. But the employment report for February showed average hourly wages had increased by a modest 0.2 percent, alleviating some near-term inflation jitters.
Although the government said non-farm payrolls grew by 339,000 jobs in February, the January and December payrolls gains were both revised downward.
In addition to monitoring wage pressures, economists said the Fed will be on guard against torrid gross domestic product (GDP) growth.
"(The Fed) is very concerned about growth," said Chris Rupkey, vice president and financial economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi.
"If growth does not slow back to 2.0 to 2.25 percent, they're going to tighten," he said. The rate hike may come at either the May 20 or July 1-2 FOMC meeting, he said.
Despite an expected increase in the fed funds target rate, many experts said the 30-year Treasury bond yield will avoid a sharp spike higher.
Analysts cited Wall Street's confidence in Greenspan, adding that an increase in short-term interest rates would be viewed as an economy-friendly, anti-inflation move.
"Once the Fed is comfortable with tightening (and does so), it will enhance their credibility," said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp.
Currently, the 30-year Treasury bond is floating near the 6.80 percent level.
"If the worst we get in a bear market is 7.25 percent to 7.35 (percent), that is a real testament to how much inflation has been wrung out of the system," Liro said.
